newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG troops drunk, asleep in Bougainville massacre.
newsitem.headline: PNG troops drunk, asleep in Bougainville massacre.

text.p: Drug abuse by soldiers and a breakdown in security, discipline and morale contributed to the massacre of 12 Papua New Guinea troops by secessionist rebels on Bougainville, a defence force report said on Thursday.
The Papua New Guinea Defence Force report on last month's killings found the rebel attack was also a result of "anger, hatred and frustration" over ill treatment of Bougainvilleans by troops.
It found resistance forces supposedly loyal to the government had assisted rebels in the attack and gunned down soldiers, some as they slept.
"The report's findings are tragic and they reveal a serious breakdown in security, discipline and morale among those security forces...," said Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan.
"There was evidence of drug abuse among soldiers and heavy consumption of home-brewed alcohol," Chan said in a statement.
Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) rebels, who have been waging a secessionist revolt for eight years, attacked the Kangu care centre on southern Bougainville island on September 8.
"The dissatisfaction among resistance force members seems to have been the trigger for the whole tragedy," said Chan.
"There have been claims that the resistance force at Kangu had been harassed and victimised," he said.

The report found that on the day of the attack, many soldiers were drunk or asleep, while others were playing volleyball. The report said many of their weapons had been carried away by resistance force members.
"The report says that soldiers had tried to retaliate, but their weapons at this stage were in the hands of the resistance fighters, who gunned them down," Chan said.
"Some bodies of these soldiers slain were later mutilated in a gruesome manner," he said.
The Kangu care centre, one of a number of refugee centres for some 70,000 Bougainvilleans, was being guarded by 32 troops when rebels attacked.
The fighting on the resource-rich island, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby, is the South Pacific's longest running armed conflict.
